results.question: Is oil export pump 10-P-1001A performing to its curve, and what happened to it in 2025?
results.answer:
**Yes. The latest data, at 2025-12-31, shows 10-P-1001A [fz-tag-6716643b6e49] on its curve: 178.3 m³/h at 440.9 m head, which is +0.1% of curve head. In 2025, though, the head fell to 7.8% below the curve by September, and replacing the wear rings put it back.** One caveat: the PI values for this pump are flagged as synthetic/modelled, so treat them as an analysis dataset, not live plant readings. The process data runs to 2025-12-31.

**Performance against the OEM curve** (model fz-equipment_model-e36023cee606, datasheet DS-SUL-200)
- The curve's best efficiency point is 190 m³/h at 430 m. Its preferred operating region is 133–228 m³/h.
- Over the last 12 months the median flow was 178.8 m³/h, 94% of the best-efficiency flow. 90% of running readings were inside the preferred region.
- Monthly head against the curve went from −0.5% (Jan 2025) to −5.3% (about June) to −7.8% (Sep). It was +0.1% in Oct, Nov and Dec.

[[figure:f_ade8ca8dc1]]
This chart shows the operating points against the OEM head and efficiency curves: head drifting down through mid-2025, then back on the curve after September.

**What happened in 2025**

| Date | Record | What |
|---|---|---|
| 05-05 to 05-11 | Incident fz-incident-8a2eeea72a83; notification 20000007 | Swapped A to C. Failed-to-start notification (contamination). **No work order linked.** |
| 09-08 to 09-12 | Incident fz-incident-be70c56f3fe0; notification 20000130 (09-11) | Swapped A to C. "Low output, head below curve" (wear). |
| 09-18 to 09-20 | WO 50000270 | Wear rings replaced and impeller inspected, cost 8,270. Head was back on the curve from October. |
| 10-15 | PM-30000005 (180-day) | Last done. Next due 2026-04-13, not overdue. |
| 12-07 to 12-14 | Incident fz-incident-6823e4976019; notification 20000144 (12-10) | High vibration. **WO 50000297 is still open** (status REL, basic finish 2026-01-09). |
| 12-24 to 12-28 | Incident fz-incident-5d7db7b9e9b0 | Swapped A to C. No notification or downtime recorded. |

All four swaps record 0 Sm³ of lost oil, because 10-P-1001C took the duty each time. Vibration was 1.79 mm/s at the latest reading, in ISO 20816 zone A (well below the 4.5 mm/s high alarm). So the measured level doesn't yet explain notification 20000144, and the vibration data only goes back to Oct 2025.

[[figure:f_1af11768c2]]
This chart shows vibration staying in zone A over the period on record.

**Gaps in the records**
- All four swaps are logged as "planned maintenance", but none has a matching work order.
- Notification 20000007 (2025) and notification 20000006 (2024 vibration) have no work order.
- WO 50000270 has no findings recorded, so the wear-ring cause is inferred, not documented.
- Head had passed the 5% loss threshold by about June, but the notification wasn't raised until September.

**Next steps (for the responsible engineer or planner)**
1. Close out WO 50000297 with findings. Its value score is about $1.2k against about $31k of effort.
2. Check whether notification 20000007 (failed to start, May 2025) still needs a work order.
3. Ask for the WO 50000270 inspection findings so the cause of the head loss is documented.
4. Consider a head-against-curve alert at about −5%, so the next wear trend is caught around June instead of September.

results.question: Why did OK-J12-02's choke stop controlling the rate in 2025?
results.answer:
The trim of production choke **72-HCV-1002** [fz-tag-437f3c54a154] wore out (eroded), so it let through more flow than it should at any given opening. Turning the choke back no longer cut the rate. The choke was replaced in October 2025, and the measured flow at a given opening is back to normal. What wore the trim out is not confirmed in the records.

**What the records show**
- **Gradual drift through 2025.** The specialists compared the choke's measured flow capacity (Cv) with the maker's curve for the same opening. In 2024 the ratio was 0.99 every quarter. In 2025 it rose to 1.08 in Q1, 1.24 in Q2 and 1.48 in Q3. The worst reading was 1.59 at 28.3% open on 2025-09-26.
- **Operator log, 2025-09-28** [fz-event-e034d9594de7]: "Choke 72-HCV-1002 at 22% but rate as at 35%; cannot trim back, suspected choke erosion; sand seen at test separator."
- **SAP notification 20000131** [fz-notification-f3c369e38908], raised 2025-09-29: "eroded, flow above characteristic", coded as internal leakage.
- **Work order 50000271** [fz-work_order-b218f462e1c1], done 2025-10-15/16: replaced the trim and body. The old Master Flo P2-12 choke, S/N CH53849 [fz-equipment-f4ce183c118b], had been in service since 2009. It was replaced with S/N CH59911 [fz-equipment-c1fb412f008c].
- **After the replacement** the ratio is back to 0.99, but that rests on only 3 readings.

[[figure:f_e9960e88e8]]
The chart shows the choke's flow capacity against the maker's curve. It sits at 0.99 through 2024, climbs through 2025 to 1.59, and drops back to 0.99 after the 2025-10-15 replacement.

**Ruled out or not supported**
- **Gas lift:** the only recorded change (13 to 12 kSm³/d, OKLOG-2025-11-20-01187 [fz-event-a5f480421425]) came after the replacement.
- **Water:** water cut rose smoothly from 23.1% to 37.8% over 2024–2025, with no sudden breakthrough.
- **Test separator or meter fault:** none is recorded. The return to 0.99 after the replacement also points to the choke, not the meter.

**Gaps in the evidence**
- **Cause of the wear:** the only evidence of sand is the operator's remark in the log. There are no sand measurements, sand probe data or sand-control history for the well. SAP codes the cause as "Corrosion", which doesn't match the suspected sand erosion.
- **No inspection report:** nothing records the condition of the removed trim.
- **No manual:** no maker's manual for the P2-12 is linked to this tag.
- **PI data is synthetic:** the wellhead pressure and choke position data are labelled synthetic, so they are not a live view.

**Worth checking next**
1. Whether the removed trim (CH53849) was inspected. A report on how it wore would separate sand erosion from corrosion and fix the SAP coding.
2. Whether the well is producing sand. Fuzer has no sand data for it, and if sand is the cause the new trim will wear the same way.
3. Over the coming months, how the new choke's flow compares with the maker's curve, to confirm the fix holds.
4. Whether the maker's P2-12 manual and a choke trim-wear procedure should be linked to this tag.

results.question: Show me the decline on OK-J07-03 and what it will make over the next year.
results.answer:
The base forecast for OK-J07-03 [fz-well-92382aee9341] is about **14,050 Sm³ of oil over the next 12 months**, counted from its latest test on 2025-12-20. The rate is expected to fall from about 42 to 35 Sm³/d. The range is roughly 12,400 to 14,700 Sm³. The fit is weak (r² 0.62), so treat these numbers as indicative.

**How the oil rate has moved**
- There are 24 monthly well tests, from 2024-01-11 to 2025-12-20.
- Oil peaked at 56.6 Sm³/d on 2024-03-11. The latest test shows 40.2 Sm³/d (`fz-well_test-13f74858bd3b`).
- Water cut has risen steadily from 33% to 54%, about 10 points a year.
- GOR has no clear trend.

[[figure:f_734e5ebeec]]
This chart shows all 24 tests: oil rate, water cut, GOR, lift gas and wellhead pressure.

**The decline fit**
- An exponential decline fits the 13 tests from 2024-12-03 to 2025-12-20.
- It starts at 51.6 Sm³/d and falls about 17% a year.
- Earlier tests were left out because of a step change. On 2024-09-03 the operator log recorded casing heading and a suspected failed-open gas lift valve (`fz-event-8f8ae6fbf831`). Oil dropped to about 30 Sm³/d and the well was shut in for 96 h (EC downtime OKDT-00014, 180 Sm³ lost). The tests show the rate back at 51.2 Sm³/d by 2024-12-03. The records don't actually show that the valve change fixed it; that is inferred.
- The fit is loose mainly because oil rate moves with lift gas. For example, lift gas was raised from 10 to 15 kSm³/d on 2025-04-25 (`fz-event-17e17baa1e2d`).

[[figure:f_1a2748de37]]
This chart shows the tests, the fitted decline and the 12-month forecast, which ends at 35.1 Sm³/d.

**What's in the forecast**
| Case | 12-month oil | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Low | ~12,400 Sm³ | Starts at the latest test rate (40.2 Sm³/d) and declines faster (nominal 0.35 a year). Hand calculation. |
| Base | 14,048 Sm³ | The fitted decline, assuming the well flows the whole time. |
| High | ~14,700 Sm³ | Starts at the fitted 42.3 Sm³/d and declines slower (nominal 0.10 a year). Hand calculation. |

- All three cases assume the well flows 100% of the time. At 98% uptime the base would be about 13,800 Sm³.
- The only recorded downtime is the 96 h in 2024. Lift gas trips in March 2024 (`fz-event-efb974183a30`, `fz-event-e42cc89025e3`) have no downtime records, so the real losses may be higher than the data shows.

**What the forecast doesn't cover**
- The decline model doesn't account for water cut speeding up, changes in lift gas supply, or another valve failure.
- I can't confirm whether the test data is current field data or historical/synthetic.

**What to check next**
1. Check whether this year's planned gas lift allocation will change the rate. A gas lift response check could narrow the range.
2. Add a water cut trend to the forecast if it keeps rising at about 10 points a year.
3. Compare the next well test with the fitted rate of about 42 Sm³/d to see whether the decline holds.

results.question: Which pipelines are losing wall thickness fastest, and why?
results.answer:
**OK-PL-005 is losing wall thickness fastest, at about 0.65 mm/yr. That is roughly four to five times faster than any other pipeline. The records don't say why.** Fuzer has no corrosion chemistry, inhibitor data, notifications, incidents or applicable documents linked to it, so any cause is inference.

**Ranking** (a straight-line fit of thickness over time at each measurement point; latest readings dated 2025-11-18)

| Pipeline | Fastest point (mm/yr) | Average (mm/yr) | Latest thickness (mm) |
|---|---|---|---|
| OK-PL-005, 8" production flowline [fz-pipeline-2850df3a14fe] | 0.70 | 0.65 | 5.5–6.4 |
| OK-PL-037, 6" production flowline [fz-pipeline-6016c8855f7e] | 0.16 | 0.09 | 8.0–8.8 |
| OK-PL-027, 10" production flowline [fz-pipeline-766793d9b930] | 0.16 | 0.10 | 10.4–10.9 |
| OK-PL-029, -033, -055, -023, -031, -008, -028 | 0.13–0.14 | 0.07–0.12 | not pulled |

**OK-PL-005 in more detail**
- Each of its 4 measurement points has 5 readings from 2019-05-10 to 2025-11-18, by UT and RT. The thinnest is 5.46 mm (`inspection:reading:TM-OK-PL-005-03-202511`).
- In 2019 it measured about 9.8–10.4 mm, so it has lost roughly 4 mm in 6.5 years.
- All four points lose wall at a similar rate (0.59–0.70 mm/yr). That suggests loss along the whole line rather than one local pit.
- The last interval looks steeper. Each point lost 0.26–0.57 mm between the Aug–Sep 2025 readings and 2025-11-18. This could be real acceleration or measurement scatter.
- From GIS (`gis:pipeline:OK-PL-005`): 2.54 km long, installed 1998, rated 70 barg, still in service.

[[figure:f_e228a80dc1]]
The chart shows OK-PL-005's thickness falling steadily at all four points since 2019.

**Why: what the records show versus inference**
- **Records:** for OK-PL-005 there are no SAP notifications or work orders, no incidents, no linked lab results (CO2, H2S, chlorides, iron, bacteria), no corrosion coupons and no inhibitor rates. None of the 12 overdue inspection plans (as of 2025-12-30) is on a pipeline. In fact, no pipeline inspection plan is linked at all.
- **Inference:** steady, even loss on a wet production flowline fits general internal CO2 corrosion of carbon steel. Nothing in the data confirms this. I didn't look into causes for the slower lines.

**Gaps**
- No minimum allowable thickness is recorded for any pipeline, so I can't estimate remaining life.
- The inspection data is loaded and healthy but only runs to 2025-11-18. It is history, not a live measurement.
- There are no earlier-conversation facts on any of the top three pipelines.

**Next steps (for the integrity engineer to decide)**
1. Get OK-PL-005's minimum allowable thickness and assess remaining life and fitness for service.
2. Consider re-measuring OK-PL-005 to confirm or rule out the late steepening.
3. Pull water cut, CO2 content and inhibitor injection records for the wells feeding OK-PL-005 to test the corrosion hypothesis.
4. Check why no pipeline inspection plans appear in SAP. They may be missing, or just not linked.

results.question: Why did 20-K-2200B keep tripping in March 2024, and what should we check if it happens again?
results.answer:
The records don't say why 20-K-2200B [fz-tag-5e3d8957c549] kept tripping. Both March trips were on high vibration, and nobody recorded a root cause. The best lead is a worn bearing or an alignment problem that wasn't fixed between the trips:
- **Lead:** the 9 March notification is coded "clearance/alignment failure", and the thrust and journal bearings were only replaced after both trips.

**What happened**

| Date | Record | What | Oil lost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 Mar | fz-incident-3f42778ed770, SAP 20000124 (raised 9 Mar) | Vibration alarm at 9 mm/s and 96 °C, no trip. Coded VIB, "clearance/alignment failure" | 0 |
| 14 Mar 03:20 | fz-incident-72f68393caf9, OKLOG-2024-03-14-00002, OKDT-00001, SAP 20000125 | Tripped on high vibration; 20-PT-3003 fell from 88 to 61 barg; down 7 h | 423 Sm³ |
| 29 Mar 22:10 | fz-incident-9367a88e752e, OKLOG-2024-03-29-00004, OKDT-00002, SAP 20000126 | Same trip; 20-PT-3003 fell from 88 to 57 barg; down 11 h | 665 Sm³ |

That's 1,088 Sm³ of oil lost over 18 h. Both trips also left gas lift wells J07, J12 and J15 short of lift gas.

**Why it kept happening**
- **No work between the trips:** neither trip notification has a work order, cause code or repair findings. The only repair was WO 50000266 [fz-work_order-9f94c3035398], replacing the thrust and journal bearings on 3–7 April, after both trips.
- **Not found:** the records have no lube oil analysis, no vibration survey and no spectra.
- **Not missed maintenance:** at 31 March 2024 no maintenance plans were overdue.
- **The repair seems to have worked:** the unit came back at 2.1 mm/s (OKLOG-2024-04-07-00006). There was no further failure until a noise report on 21 September 2025 (SAP 20000078). That was coded "clearance/alignment" again and fixed by tightening the baseplate bolts (WO 50000161).

The repeat alignment code points to looseness or alignment, but that isn't proven. The sister unit 20-K-2200A also needed its baseplate bolts tightened (WO 50000095). Its trips were traced to a faulty trip transmitter (WO 50000088) and a trip setpoint change (WO 50000093), so B's trip instruments were never checked for the same thing.

[[figure:f_aab4aa354a]]
The chart shows vibration rising from 1 March and staying above the 7.1 mm/s high-high alarm before both trips. **This is synthetic model data, not PI:** Fuzer has no PI connection. It also disagrees with the logged 96 °C, so don't treat it as evidence. It also suggests a third stop on 1 April that no log, downtime or notification record mentions.

**What to check if it trips again** (for the responsible engineer and operator, under site procedures)
1. **Bearings and trend before any restart:** check bearing temperatures and the vibration trend. Two trips in 30 days calls for a bearing inspection (TG-20-001 rev A, "Symptoms and actions"). March met that criterion, but no inspection was done.
2. **Alignment and foundation:** check alignment, baseplate bolt tightness and the anti-surge controller (OEM-C40 rev A §5 p.5; §3 p.3 for foundation and alignment). Also check the rotor balance, which was the fix on 2200A (WO 50000092).
3. **Trip instruments:** check the vibration probe, the trip transmitter and the trip setpoint, as was done on 2200A.
4. **Restart prerequisites** (PR-CO-001 rev A §2 p.2): check lube oil and seal gas, and take an oil sample.
5. **Record the cause:** put cause and damage codes on the notification. None were recorded in March.

The data runs to 30 December 2025. As of then, the 180-day PM PM-30000026 is 179 days overdue. Overhaul WO 50000306 (bearings, dry gas seals, impeller inspection) is open at priority 2, and a vibration route is due in about 22 days. The value score suggests a root cause analysis before a permanent fix. Whether to do one is for the reliability team.

results.question: What was our production efficiency in 2025, and what were the biggest losses?
results.answer:
Production efficiency for 2025 was **99.3%**: 2,761,933 Sm³ of oil produced against 2,782,106 Sm³ of potential (EC DAY001, all 12 months). By far the biggest loss was the planned GGCP and PP shutdown in June. Unplanned losses were small.

**One caveat before you use these numbers:** the gap to potential (20,173 Sm³) is smaller than the deferment recorded in EC downtime (34,328 Sm³). The two sources don't agree, so 99.3% should be quoted as the DAY001 figure, not as a checked result. The data is also very regular (for example, lift gas is flat at 1,800 kSm³/d), so it may be modelled or synthetic rather than measured. The sources were last loaded 2026-11-09, report no failing checks, and cover all of 2025.

**Biggest losses in 2025 (EC downtime, 16 events, 34,328 Sm³ in total)**

| Reason | Lost oil (Sm³) | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Planned maintenance: GGCP and PP shutdown, OKDT-00025 [fz-downtime-5d760b357bbd], 1–5 June, 96 h | 32,800 | 95.5% |
| Well interventions (8 events) | 598 | 1.7% |
| EGP export curtailment (2 events) | 550 | 1.6% |
| Process trips on 20-K-2300A [fz-tag-4aa94b402c01] (2 events) | 200 | 0.6% |
| Gas lift valve failure, OK-J07-05 [fz-well-fc71d57aa6b8], 15 April | 180 | 0.5% |

[[figure:f_8b2953b090]]
The chart ranks deferred oil by reason for 2025. Planned maintenance makes up almost all of it.

**The one repeat failure:** compressor 20-K-2300A tripped twice on high discharge temperature because its after-cooler was fouled:
- 24 June [fz-incident-876328991e4a]: 100 Sm³ lost.
- 16 July [fz-incident-5eb815dbd857], OKDT-00007: 100 Sm³ lost.

On 16 July an eddy current inspection of 20-E-2350A [fz-incident-f4ec53cad8f9] also found thinned tubes and a cooler that had "fouled again". The volume is small, but the same cause came back within a month.

**Month by month:** efficiency was 99–100% in most months. The low months were:
- **June, 96.7%:** this is the shutdown. Even so, the DAY001 gap that month (7,323 Sm³) is much smaller than the 32,900 Sm³ of deferment recorded.
- **October, 97.6%:** about 5,830 Sm³ is missing against potential, and there are no deferment records for it. This loss is unexplained.
- **August, 98.9%.**

**Suggested next checks**
1. Ask whoever owns EC (Energy Components) how DAY001 potential is set, and whether planned shutdowns are already taken out of it. That would explain the mismatch with the downtime records.
2. Find out what caused October's ~5,830 Sm³ gap. Nothing in the downtime or incident records accounts for it.
3. Ask Maintenance & Integrity to look at the 20-E-2350A after-cooler: fouling, thinned tubes, and what it does to 20-K-2300A.
4. Load the downtime reason and SAP maintenance code tables (`ec_downtime_reasons` and `sap_maintenance_codes`, currently "not loaded"). Losses could then be sorted by equipment: right now less than 1% of the lost oil is tied to a tag.

results.question: How did oil production trend through 2025, and what explains the changes?
results.answer:
Oil production stayed close to flat through 2025 and eased slightly. The allocated rate was about 7,595 Sm³/d in January and 7,486 Sm³/d in December, down 1.4%. The year totalled 2,761,933 Sm³ against a potential of 2,782,106 Sm³, which is 99.3% efficiency. That comes from EC DAY001 allocated oil and EC downtime, loaded and healthy as of 2026-11-09. Only one dip clearly traces to lost production: the planned shutdown in June. The rest of the drift looks like the wells declining gradually, not downtime.

**Month by month (Sm³/d):** Jan 7,595 · Feb 7,926 (peak) · Mar 7,877 · Apr 7,405 · May 7,535 · Jun 7,071 (low) · Jul 7,339 · Aug 7,815 · Sep 7,728 · Oct 7,720 · Nov 7,565 · Dec 7,486

[[figure:f_3610bc4ce7]]
Monthly actual vs potential oil rate. The chart was drawn from the monthly summary figures, not straight from the records.

**What explains the changes**
- **June shutdown (the main loss).** 34,328 Sm³ of oil was lost in 2025, and 32,800 Sm³ of it (95.5%) came from one planned event. That was the plant shutdown recorded as downtime OKDT-00025 [fz-downtime-5d760b357bbd], 2025-06-01 to 06-05 (96 h).
- **Unplanned losses were small, about 1,528 Sm³ for the year:**
  - well interventions: 598 Sm³
  - export curtailment: 550 Sm³
  - two compressor trips on 20-K-2300A [fz-tag-4aa94b402c01]: 200 Sm³
  - one gas lift valve failure on OK-J07-05 [fz-well-fc71d57aa6b8]: 180 Sm³

[[figure:f_3306ca3966]]
Deferred oil by reason. Planned maintenance dominates.

- **Wells declining across the field.** All the largest well-level changes are declines; no well showed a gain. Every well-level figure below comes from well tests, roughly monthly, with the latest in December 2025.
  - The top decliners lost about 24–43% of their oil rate. The next 25 lost 14–23%.
  - Water cut rose by roughly 6–10 points in most of these wells.
  - OK-J09-05 [fz-well-426deb42033d] fits a decline of about 13.9% a year.

[[figure:f_fbe1df7e94]]
Oil-rate change by well, top 10 decliners.

- **OK-J03-02 [fz-well-5b8a07c2175c] is the one step change.** Oil fell from 86.7 to 51.8 Sm³/d between the 2025-05-04 and 2025-06-08 tests, and water cut jumped from 26% to 72%. Water cut then kept climbing to 87% by December.
  - Lab results support more produced water: chloride rose from about 16,000 to 34,000 mg/L.
  - The operator log OKLOG-2025-06-12-02427 says "water breakthrough suspected", but nobody has confirmed that.
- **Gas lift was steady.** Lift gas held at about 1,800 kSm³/d, and I found no allocation changes in 2025.

**Gaps and inconsistencies**
- **Two unexplained steps.** Production dropped about 470 Sm³/d from March to April and rose about 476 Sm³/d from July to August. Neither matches any recorded deferment, so both are unexplained.
- **Unexplained shortfalls.** October came in 5,830 Sm³ below potential with no reason recorded, and August 2,608 Sm³ below with only 133 Sm³ recorded.
- **Well tests and allocation disagree.** The latest well tests add up to 9,528 Sm³/d, against 7,486 Sm³/d allocated in December, which suggests an allocation factor of about 0.79. The two figures haven't been reconciled.
- **OK-J03-02 lift gas.** Its tests show 0 lift gas, but operator logs record gas lift increases on that well. One of the two sources is wrong.
- **Not covered.** Back-pressure wasn't analysed, and how much of the year's drift comes from decline hasn't been quantified.

**Suggested next checks**
1. Production engineer: compare tests with allocation (factor about 0.79) and find the cause of the October and August gaps.
2. Subsurface engineer: decide whether OK-J03-02 is water breakthrough or coning, and check its real lift gas setting.
3. Quantify how much of the year's drift comes from decline, and size the gas lift reallocation. Within each header, the wells that respond least to lift gas (OK-J07-05) would give gas to those that respond most (OK-J02-02, OK-J12-09, OK-J17-01).
4. Review the 11 incidents not yet looked at, from the 21 recorded.

results.question: What has been limiting production over the last two years, and how does it cascade through the field?
results.answer:
Over 2024-01-01 to 2025-12-30, most recorded lost oil came from two planned shutdowns. Equipment failures cost little oil but repeat often, and almost all of them are on the gas compressors. These compressors feed one lift gas header that serves 142 gas-lifted wells. Two other limits never show up as lost-oil records: how lift gas is shared between wells, and separator back-pressure. Together they hold back more oil than all the trips. The data runs to 2025-12-30 and is synthetic, not live.

**Recorded lost oil: 69,751 Sm³ (33 downtime records)**

| Reason | Oil lost (Sm³) |
|---|---|
| Planned shutdowns (2024-04; 2025-06-01 to 05, OKDT-00025) | 65,600 (94%) |
| Well interventions (16 events) | 1,436 |
| Lift gas shortfall: 20-K-2200B vibration trips 2024-03-14 and 03-29 (OKDT-00001/00002) | 1,088 |
| Process trips: five 20-K-2300A high-temperature trips (425) plus carry-over from separator 20-V-2001 that tripped train C in Nov 2024 (292) | 717 |
| Gas export curtailment, Feb–Mar 2025 | 550 |

[[figure:f_53422ef7ed]]
The first chart ranks lost oil by reason; planned shutdowns dominate it. Unplanned losses fell from about 2,600 Sm³ in 2024 to about 1,500 Sm³ in 2025. Gas export curtailment is the only reason that got worse.

**How a trip spreads**
1. Compressors 20-K-2300A/B/C and separator 20-V-2001 feed lift gas header 20-FT-3002.
2. That header feeds 48 wells directly and the two downstream headers, 30-FT-3002 (60 wells) and 40-FT-3002 (34 wells).
3. When 20-K-2200B tripped, header pressure 20-PT-3003 fell from 88 to 57 barg (operator log OKLOG-2024-03-29-00004). Wells on jackets J07, J12 and J15 lost lift.
4. Jackets that get their lift gas through another jacket (for example J12 via J09) are at the end of the line and lose it first.

One gap: the data graph does not link 20-K-2200B to the header. That connection comes only from the logs and the downtime comments.

**Oil held back with no lost-oil record** (board estimates over 90 days):
- **Sharing lift gas better between wells:**
  - on 30-FT-3002: 11,745 Sm³ ($5.52M)
  - on 20-FT-3002: 8,073 Sm³
  - on 40-FT-3002: 7,551 Sm³
- **Lower separator pressure:**
  - 30-V-2002 down 0.8 bar: 8,055 Sm³. That separator collects about 70 wells, all limited by back-pressure. Some wells, such as those on J05 and J10, are hit by both limits.
  - 40-V-2002 down 0.69 bar: 3,546 Sm³.

**Why the risk is still live**
- Compressors had 33 failures on 9 units, a failure every 199 days per unit on average.
  - 20-K-2200B failed again on 2025-09-21, after new bearings in April 2024.
  - Noise faults keep coming back after "tighten baseplate bolts" fixes.
- Planned maintenance is overdue on several of these compressors: 20-K-2200B by 179 days (PM-30000026), 20-K-2300A by 104 days. Four of them are rated extreme risk.
- 20-K-2300A runs at 120.1 °C discharge against a 134 °C trip limit, the tightest margin found.
- Inspection of separator 20-V-2001 is 91 days overdue.

[[figure:f_6c2af0d439]]
The second chart counts failures by unit: the compressor trains lead.

**Caveats**

results.question: Which wells lost the most oil rate in 2025, and why?
results.answer:
OK-J03-02 lost the most oil in 2025, about 38–43 Sm³/d, because water broke through in June. The next four wells each lost 13–21 Sm³/d between their first and latest 2025 tests. For them, the records point to a slow rise in water cut plus less lift gas on recent tests, not to the reservoir or the facility. Test data runs to 2025-12-21.

[[figure:f_ad2bde01a4]]
The chart ranks wells by oil change from first to latest 2025 test. J03-02 is −42.7, and the next nine are bunched between −22 and −26. Two caveats: the chart doesn't give units, and those middle-group figures are bigger than the test-based drops below. The test records give J03-02's drop as 37.7 Sm³/d (88.2 → 50.5), so the ranking probably starts from a different baseline test.

| Well | Oil, first → latest test (Sm³/d) | Water cut | What the records show |
|---|---|---|---|
| OK-J03-02 | 88.2 → 50.5 | 26% → 87% | Oil stepped down by about 36 Sm³/d between 2025-05-04 and 2025-06-08 (test fz-well_test-0c7019983ddd). Operator log OKLOG-2025-06-12-02427 says "water breakthrough suspected". Chloride at the wellhead roughly doubled. The well has no gas lift. |
| OK-J09-05 | 59.8 → 44.5 | 52% → 61% | Lift gas fell from about 19 to 6.8 kSm³/d and oil rose and fell with it. Fuzer's gas lift check estimates about +7 Sm³/d with more gas. |
| OK-J06-02 | 68 → 51.0 | 45% → 52% | The latest test (2025-12-14) was taken on low lift gas (6.6 kSm³/d). |
| OK-J13-01 | ~82 → 61.8 | 47% → 56% | Lift gas has been below 11 kSm³/d since September. Part of the loss is a real trend. |
| OK-J12-03 | 51.2 → 38.9 | 21% → 31% | The low tests were taken on low gas. On 2025-11-21 it made 46.9 Sm³/d at 19.7 kSm³/d. |

[[figure:f_2f1404b16d]]
This chart shows oil rate by test for these five wells. The specialist typed the values in from the test records, so the chart has no source link of its own. It shows J03-02's June step and the gas-driven scatter on the other four.

[[figure:f_dca1afcb48]]
This chart shows J03-02's water cut, chloride and other test values climbing after the breakthrough.

**What the records rule out**
- **Deferment:** none of the 10 wells has an EC deferment record in 2025. 95.5% of the 34,328 Sm³ deferred was one planned shutdown that hit the whole facility (OKDT-00025, 2025-06-01 to 06-05).
- **Lift gas supply:** no shortfall is recorded. The only compression events are two short 20-K-2300A trips (OKDT-00006 and OKDT-00007).
- **Other causes:** GOR shows no trend. Reservoir pressure and completion data aren't in Fuzer.

**Caveats**
- Ranking on first vs latest test exaggerates the loss on gas-lifted wells when the last test was on low gas. Except for J03-02, the "loss" is partly gas allocation.
- The records don't show why lift gas fell on these wells.
- Wells ranked 6–10 (J19-05, J07-03, J17-05, J16-03, J01-05) weren't reviewed one by one.

**Possible next steps**
1. Production engineer: screen OK-J03-02 for a water-control or intervention candidate. Nothing in the records explains where the water is coming from.
2. Production engineer: review lift gas for J09-05, J13-01 and J12-03 against open gas lift opportunities 30–32. J13-01 is a named receiver, with about 20 Sm³/d of gain for about 12.6 kSm³/d. Those items say a step-rate test is needed before any gas is moved.
3. Find out why lift gas on these wells dropped during 2025. It could be allocation decisions or a supply issue on the headers that feed them (20-, 30- and 40-FT-3002).
4. Review wells 6–10 in the same way, and confirm the baseline the ranking uses.

results.question: Who are our bad actors over the last two years, and what are their repeat failure modes?
results.answer:
The bad actors are the gas compressors. Five compressors and the 10-P-1001A pump had **4–5 corrective failures each** between 2023-12-30 and 2025-12-30, the two years up to the last day in the data. The repeat modes are **spurious stops (UST), noise (NOI), vibration (VIB) and overheating (OHE)**. The pattern runs across the whole compressor class, not one unit. These are historical records to 2025-12-30, not live data.

| Tag | Failures | Lost oil (Sm³) | Mode that repeats | Behind it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20-K-2200B | 5 | 1,088 | UST ×3 | SAP notifs 20000077, 20000125, 20000126. The March 2024 trips were on high vibration and lost 423 + 665 Sm³ (incidents fz-incident-72f68393caf9, fz-incident-9367a88e752e) |
| 20-K-2300C | 5 | 0 | NOI ×3 | 20000113, 20000116, 20000115. Noise came back after bearing changes in Nov 2024 and Feb 2025 |
| 20-K-2100B | 5 | 0 | NOI ×2 | 20000065, 20000068. Noise came back after the bearing job on WO 50000142 |
| 20-K-2300A | 4 | 425 | UST ×3 | 20000048, 20000050, 20000049. The trips followed fouling of after-cooler 20-E-2350A, which has OHE ×2 |
| 10-P-1001A | 4 | 0 | VIB ×2 | 20000006 (2024-09) and 20000144 (2025-12) |
| 20-K-2100C | 3 | 0 | OHE ×2 | 20000098, 20000140. It came back after the tube clean on WO 50000202 |

20-K-2200A (4 failures) and 20-K-2200C (3) each had several different modes, but none repeated.

[[figure:f_bec1783cb4]]
The chart ranks corrective notifications by tag. The compressor and pump classes take all of the top eight places.

**This is a class-wide problem.** The compressor class (ISO14224:CO.CE) has 9 units, 33 failures in the window and an MTBF of about 199 days, with no single outlier. 20-K-2200B is a Solar Turbines C40 (fz-equipment-d3478d5cc473). The specialist did not check the other units' models.

**Overdue work on these units:**
- PM plans: PM-30000026 on 20-K-2200B (179 days overdue), PM-30000016 on 20-K-2200A (134), PM-30000019 on 20-K-2300A (104), and others 31–67 days overdue.
- Value score puts 20-K-2200B, 20-K-2300A and 20-K-2200A in the **extreme** risk band ($62k, $49k and $49k).
- Open work orders 50000303, 50000282, 50000289, 50000299 and 50000287 are 58–126 days overdue.

**The counts are probably too low:**
- Five high discharge-temperature trips on 20-K-2300A (2024-06 to 2025-07) have EC downtime records but no SAP notification, so they aren't counted.
- Some codes contradict the incident text. 20-K-2300A trips are coded "Vibration" although the text says high temperature. 10-P-1001A planned swaps are coded VIB/FTS/LOO.
- Several notifications have no work order, including 20000077, 20000125 and 20000126.
- The SAP failure-code table (`sap_maintenance_codes`) and the EC downtime-reason table (`ec_downtime_reasons`) have never been loaded, so code meanings and deferment reasons can't be checked against them. Lost oil here comes from EC downtime only.

**Next steps:**
1. Reliability engineer: do a root-cause review of compressor bearing and noise failures across the class, starting with 20-K-2300C and 20-K-2100B.
2. Decide whether the 20-K-2300A trips should be treated as an after-cooler fouling problem rather than a compressor one.
3. Planner: review the overdue compressor PMs, starting with PM-30000026.
4. Clean up the coding and raise notifications for the 20-K-2300A trips so future counts are reliable.

results.question: How is lift gas distributed across the headers, and where would moving lift gas between wells gain the most oil?
results.answer:
The most oil from moving lift gas is on the **ST1 header (30-FT-3002)**, which has the most gas, the most wells and the biggest reallocation gain. The model estimates about **+130 Sm³/d of oil** there without adding any gas. GGCP and ST2 would each gain about 84–90 Sm³/d. All figures are from well tests up to December 2025, not live data. The value scoring is as of 2025-12-30.

**How the lift gas is split** (sums of each well's latest well test)

| Header | Jackets | Wells on gas lift | Lift gas (kSm³/d) | Oil (Sm³/d) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GGCP 20-FT-3002 [fz-tag-9d03fb29f26f] | 9 | 48 | 626.6 | 2,697 |
| ST1 30-FT-3002 [fz-tag-613c0b396797] | 10 | 60 | 723.8 | 3,280 |
| ST2 40-FT-3002 [fz-tag-ea95fa6bd715] | 6 | 34 | 443.9 | 1,825 |

- GGCP is supplied by vessel 20-V-2001 and compressors 20-K-2300A/B/C. It feeds the ST1 and ST2 headers and its own gas lift manifolds (NWP-GLM, OKJ01/03/06/23-GLM…), according to the lift gas network trace.
- So the 20-FT-3002 meter should carry gas for all three headers. The table splits it by the wells each header serves, about 1,794 kSm³/d in total.
- Fuzer has no figure for compressor or header capacity, so I can't say how much spare gas there is.

**Where moving gas gains most** (value_score; each move takes gas from wells past the 0.5 Sm³ oil per kSm³ optimum and gives it to wells short of it, with the header total unchanged)

| Opportunity | Moves | Gas moved | Oil gain | 90-day value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| scan:gas_lift:30-FT-3002 | 21 | 71.2 kSm³/d | +130.5 Sm³/d | $5.5M |
| scan:gas_lift:20-FT-3002 | 20 | 62.9 kSm³/d | +89.7 Sm³/d | $3.8M |
| scan:gas_lift:40-FT-3002 | 17 | 64.9 kSm³/d | +83.9 Sm³/d | $3.5M |

- **ST1:** the biggest moves take gas from OK-J11-03 (10.4 kSm³/d) and OK-J07-05 (6.9 kSm³/d) and give it to OK-J12-09. They add about 23 and 16 Sm³/d.
  - OK-J07-05 gets *less* oil the more gas it gets (−1.25 Sm³ oil per extra kSm³). That may mean a gas lift valve problem; it is worth checking before treating it as spare gas.
- **GGCP:** OK-J08-04 → OK-J06-06, 10.7 kSm³/d for about +21 Sm³/d.
- **ST2:** OK-J24-02 → OK-J17-02, 9.3 kSm³/d for about +15 Sm³/d.

[[figure:f_a46135d5cc]]
The chart shows how much extra oil each well gets per extra unit of lift gas, grouped by header. Wells above 0.5 Sm³/kSm³ are short of gas; wells below it are giving it away.

**Limits on these estimates**
- All three are medium confidence. They come from the scatter in well tests, and the effort cost ($3k) is a default assumption.
- Moves were only modelled within a header, not between headers.
- Some receiving wells get their gas through another jacket's manifold, which could limit the gain. Examples: OK-J12-09 via OKAN-69 and OK-J02-02 via OKAN-63.
- I didn't check open incidents on the donor and receiving wells. Injection meter readings weren't used.

**Suggested next steps** (the decisions are yours)
1. Production engineering: check the OK-J07-05 response and its valves before using it as a donor.
2. Run step-rate tests on the top ST1 receivers (OK-J12-09 first), then well tests after any move, as each opportunity record recommends.
3. Confirm compressor and header capacity outside Fuzer before also looking at moves between headers.

results.question: Why does lift gas keep running short, and what should go in the next turnaround to fix it?
results.answer:
# Why lift gas keeps running short, and what to put in OK-TAR-2026

**Why it runs short.** Lift gas runs short in two ways, and only one of them needs the turnaround.

1. **Repeat trips on two compressors, a supply problem.** This is the cause the records actually name.
2. **Uneven sharing of the gas across wells, an allocation problem.** No shutdown is needed for this one. It is worth more oil than the trips cost, but it is my inference that it explains the shortages you see.

The data runs to 2025-12-31.

## The trips

Between 2024 and 2025 there were 9 compression trips that hit lift gas. Together they lost about 1,805 Sm³ of oil, under 3% of total deferment.
[[figure:f_a5412ef216]]
The chart ranks deferred oil by cause tag. 20-K-2200B is the largest cause, then 20-K-2300A, then the 20-V-2001 carryover events.

| Cause | Events | Lost oil | What the records say |
|---|---|---|---|
| **20-K-2200B** [fz-tag-5e3d8957c549], train B 2nd stage | 2 high-vibration trips, March 2024 (OKDT-00001, OKDT-00002) | 1,088 Sm³ | Vibration reached 9 mm/s, above the 7.1 mm/s trip limit. Header pressure 20-PT-3003 fell to 57 barg (operator log 2024-03-29). J07, J12 and J15 wells went short. The bearings were replaced in April 2024 (WO 50000266). No trips since. |
| **20-K-2300A** [fz-tag-4aa94b402c01] | 5 high discharge temperature trips, 2024-06-11 to 2025-07-16 (OKDT-00003 to 00007) | 425 Sm³ | Discharge temperature hit 168–171 °C. The logs blame after-cooler 20-E-2350A: "fouled again, eddy current found thinned tubes". Cleaning hasn't held (WOs 50000267, 50000268). |
| **20-V-2001 carryover** tripping train C | 2 trips, November 2024 (OKDT-00008, 00009) | 292 Sm³ | High level in 20-V-2101C caused by liquid carried over from 20-V-2001. |

- **Not proven:** that fouling is the only cause on 20-K-2300A. Earlier repairs replaced trip transmitters (WOs 50000108, 50000110), so some trips may come from the instrument.
- **20-K-2200B is a hidden dependency.** Fuzer's lift gas network model does not link it to the header, but its trips clearly starve the header.

## Allocation

The three lift gas headers feed 142 wells with about 1,794 kSm³/d of gas. Some wells use gas with almost no oil response, for example OK-J07-05 and OK-J09-01. Moving gas to the best responders is scored at about +304 Sm³/d of oil across the three headers (value_score items 30–32). This needs no shutdown, but each move must first be confirmed by step-rate tests and well tests.

## Turnaround scope (OK-TAR-2026, starts 2026-04-06, all orders still CRTD)

These are inputs for the planner and the turnaround team to decide on, not decisions.

**Already in scope. Keep these:**
- WO 50000307, retube 20-E-2350A. This targets the 20-K-2300A trips.
- WO 50000306, overhaul of 20-K-2200B. The gasket set MAT-100036 for this job has **zero stock**, so it needs ordering in time for April.
- WO 50000308, internal inspection of 20-V-2001 and replacement of its level bridle. This targets the carryover trips.

**Gaps to consider adding:**
- **INSP-30000009**, the statutory internal inspection of lift gas scrubber 20-V-2002. It is 168 days overdue, needs a shutdown, and is not in scope.
- Other overdue vessel inspections that are not in scope: 20-V-2301C (290 days overdue), 20-V-2201C (198 days) and 20-V-2101B (137 days).
- Notification 20000049 on 20-K-2300A (spurious stop, 2025-11-15) has no work order yet. Checking the trip instrument during the window would cover the transmitter question above.

The overdue preventive maintenance on 20-K-2200B, 20-K-2300A and 20-K-2300C does not need a shutdown. It can be done before the turnaround.

## Gaps in the data
- The data has no compressor capacities, so I can't confirm whether there is a spare train to cover a trip.
- Header flow and pressure trends around each trip were not checked.
- Process values are modelled, not live.

## Next steps
1. The planner decides on adding INSP-30000009 and expediting MAT-100036.
2. Root-cause analysis on 20-K-2300A covering both the cooler and the trip instrument, before the retube design is fixed.
3. Production engineering screens the reallocation moves with step-rate tests.

I can draft any of these as work items for confirmation on the page.

**In short:** OKAN produced **2,761,933 Sm³ of oil** in 2025 (about 7,588 Sm³/d). That is 99.3 % of the 2,782,106 Sm³ potential and about 2 % lower per day than 2024. Losses were almost all one planned shutdown in June. The work backlog is old and much of it is overdue. The data runs to 2025-12-30 and was loaded 2026-11-09; none of it is live.

## Production (EC daily production, `ec_day001`)

- **Water:** no figures came back. I did not check day by day for zero-production days.

[[figure:f_757565b2d6]]
Monthly 2025 oil against deferment. The specialist typed these numbers in by hand from the production summary.

## Losses (EC downtime, 33 records)
- **Total deferred oil:** 34,328 Sm³.
  - **Planned maintenance:** 32,800 Sm³ (95.5 %), from one 96 h event ending 2025-06-01. June efficiency was 96.7 %.
  - **Unplanned:** 1,528 Sm³ altogether:

| Cause | Lost oil |
|---|---|
| Well interventions (8 events) | 598 Sm³ |
| EGP export curtailment | 550 Sm³ |
| Process trips (2 trips of 20-K-2300A [fz-tag-4aa94b402c01], last 2025-07-16) | 200 Sm³ |
| Gas lift valve failure | 180 Sm³ |

- **Worst well:** OK-J07-05 [fz-well-fc71d57aa6b8], 180 Sm³.

[[figure:f_76a3119322]]
Deferment Pareto by reason. One bar dominates: planned maintenance. The chart shows its share as 98.9 %, not the 95.5 % worked out from the total, so the chart's base needs checking.

## Work backlog (SAP, as of 2026-11-09)
- **Open work orders:** 37, all more than 180 days old (6 P2, 17 P3, 14 P4). 5 are in the 2026 turnaround (OK-TAR-2026).
  - Oldest: 50000298 (P4, 2025-07-03).

2. **Loss attribution is thin.** The 32,800 Sm³ June event is not linked to any well or equipment, and there is no incident record for it. Only one equipment tag has any loss attributed to it.

   - EC downtime reason codes, so losses by reason are coarse.

results.question: There is a gas release on the jacket right now. What should the crew do?

args.question: gas release emergency response jacket muster ESD

results.answer:
I can't direct an emergency response, and Fuzer has no gas-release emergency procedure for me to point you to. The crew should follow your site's emergency response plan and do what the OIM / person in charge and the control room tell them. Right now that usually means:

- **Raise the alarm and report it** through the site's normal route (control room, PA, manual alarm point) if that hasn't already happened. Say where the release is, how big it looks, and which way the wind is blowing.
- **Follow the site's alarm response and muster instructions.** Get out of the gas area by the safe route, going upwind or crosswind, and keep away from ignition sources.
- **Leave decisions to the people with emergency authority.** Shutdown, isolation, blowdown and whether anyone goes back into the area are calls for the control room, OIM and emergency response team, made under your procedures.

**What I checked:** I searched Fuzer's documents for gas release, emergency response and muster guidance. The only matches were a lift gas shortfall troubleshooting guide (TG-20L-001 rev A), an NWP gas producer guide (TG-50-001 rev A) and a gas turbine OEM manual. None of these is an emergency procedure, so don't use them for this. Fuzer also gets its data in batches, not live, so I can't see what is happening on the jacket now.

**Once people are safe and the situation is under control,** I can help with:
1. Which jacket it is, what equipment and wells are connected to it, and what flows to and from it.
2. The process values, alarms and log entries leading up to the release, from the most recent data Fuzer has.
3. A timeline from the records and any past releases on the same equipment, to support the investigation.

Tell me which jacket or tag it is and I'll start when you're ready.
